beats.intro: Derivatives, module two. [[sub]]Forwards, futures, swaps, options and credit derivatives: how each one works, and what each one pays.
beats.forward: [[a]]Forwards, futures and swaps are firm commitments: both sides must perform, at a price agreed in advance. [[line]]Start with a forward. The buyer gains when the spot price at maturity is above the forward price, and loses when it is below. The payoff is the spot price minus the forward price, a straight line. The seller gets the mirror image. [[ex]]Procam agrees to buy one hundred ounces of gold at seventeen ninety-two dollars and thirteen cents. [[st]]At maturity, gold is at seventeen eighty dollars and fifty cents. [[pay]]The payoff is negative eleven dollars sixty-three per ounce. [[tot]]Times one hundred ounces, Procam pays eleven hundred sixty-three dollars.
beats.futures: [[a]]A futures contract is a standardized forward traded on an exchange, with one big difference: daily settlement. [[mtm]]Each day the clearinghouse marks the contract to market, and moves gains and losses through margin accounts. [[init]]Procam posts forty-nine fifty of initial margin, and must keep at least forty-five hundred, the maintenance margin. [[d4]]Four days before maturity, gold futures fall, and the balance drops to forty-three sixty-two, below maintenance. A margin call of five hundred eighty-eight dollars restores it. [[d2]]Another fall two days before maturity brings a second call, of eight hundred eighty. [[tot]]In total, Procam pays fourteen sixty-eight in margin calls, and gets three hundred five back at the end. The net loss is eleven sixty-three, the same as the forward, just paid in pieces.
beats.swaps: [[a]]A swap is a firm commitment to exchange a series of cash flows. In the most common one, an interest rate swap, one side pays a fixed rate and the other pays a floating rate. [[ex]]Fyleton has a two hundred million pound swap. It receives fixed at two point two five percent, and pays the six-month floating rate. [[fix]]The fixed payment for six months is two million, two hundred fifty thousand pounds. [[flt]]If the floating rate is one point nine five percent, Fyleton owes one million, nine hundred fifty thousand. [[net]]The two are netted: Fyleton receives three hundred thousand pounds. [[note]]The notional is never exchanged. And, like a forward, a swap starts with a value of zero.
beats.options: [[a]]An option is a contingent claim: the buyer has a right, not an obligation. A call gives the right to buy. [[prem]]Say the buyer pays a premium of five dollars, for the right to buy at a strike price of thirty. [[s1]]If the stock ends at forty, the buyer exercises. The payoff is ten dollars, and the profit is five, after the premium. [[s2]]If it ends at twenty-five, the buyer walks away, and loses only the five-dollar premium. [[be]]The break-even is the strike plus the premium: thirty-five. [[fm]]The payoff is the larger of zero and S T minus X. It can never be negative.
beats.profiles: [[a]]Here is the long call again, next to its mirror image, the short call. The seller collects the premium, but faces unlimited loss as the price rises. [[lp]]A put gives the right to sell. The long put gains as the price falls: its payoff is the larger of zero and X minus S T. [[sp]]The short put keeps at most the premium. Its loss can be large, but is limited, because a price cannot fall below zero. [[sum]]Buyers risk only the premium. Sellers can risk far more.
beats.credit: [[a]]A credit default swap is a contingent claim on a borrower's default. [[prem]]The protection buyer pays a fixed spread, like an insurance premium. [[ev]]If a credit event happens, such as bankruptcy or failure to pay, the seller pays the buyer the loss given default times the notional. [[mig]]Before any default, spreads move. If the spread widens from one hundred to two hundred fifty basis points, the buyer, who locked in the cheap spread, gains, and the seller loses. [[ins]]It works like insurance: a hedge for a bondholder, or a bet on weaker credit for someone who holds no bond.
beats.compare: [[a]]Now compare the two families. [[lin]]A forward has a straight-line payoff. Both sides can win or lose, and nothing is paid upfront. [[non]]A call option has a kinked payoff. The buyer pays a premium upfront, and in return can lose no more than that premium. [[cmp]]Both gain when the underlying rises. The call is like owning the underlying with downside protection, paid for by the premium. [[cross]]Below the crossing point, the option does better. Above it, the forward does better.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Forwards, futures and swaps are firm commitments with straight-line payoffs. [[w2]]Futures settle daily through margin. Swaps exchange net cash flows. [[w3]]An option gives the buyer a choice. Its payoff is the larger of zero and S T minus X for a call, or X minus S T for a put. [[w4]]Options are non-linear, and a credit default swap insures against default.
